_about: Question bank seeds: curious neurology and psychiatry (incl. Oliver Sacks). Each item = a checked core fact for puzzle writers to turn into questions (Triviosis, Grand Rounds, Zebritis, Dxtective, Word of the week). Tone: fascinated, respectful, never mocking patients. Re-check details against a reputable source before publishing; write all wording fresh.

sacks.topic: The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat (1985)
sacks.fact: Title case 'Dr P.', a music teacher with visual agnosia: he could see shapes but not recognise objects or faces, and reached for his wife's head as if it were his hat.
Jimmie G., a former navy sailor with Korsakoff syndrome (alcohol-related thiamine deficiency), believed it was still 1945 and could not form new memories.
A man with Tourette syndrome who was a brilliant jazz drummer; on haloperidol his tics settled but so did his spontaneity, so he chose to take it only on weekdays.
Identical twin brothers with autism who swapped large prime numbers as a game; Sacks described them in The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat.
Survivors of the 1917–1928 encephalitis lethargica epidemic, frozen for decades, briefly 'awoke' on L-dopa in 1969 at Beth Abraham Hospital, New York. Robin Williams played Sacks in the film.
Orthopaedic surgeon Tony Cicoria was struck by lightning from a payphone in 1994 and soon developed a sudden passion for piano music and composing.
People losing vision can see vivid, silent hallucinations (faces, patterns, little people) while knowing they are not real. Named after Charles Bonnet, who described his grandfather in 1760.
Title phrase comes from Temple Grandin, an autistic animal scientist, describing how she felt among other people.

sacks.topic: The Case of the Colorblind Painter
sacks.fact: An artist ('Jonathan I.') lost all colour vision after a car crash (cerebral achromatopsia): the world turned shades of grey.
On Pingelap atoll in Micronesia, about 1 in 12 people have achromatopsia (total colour blindness), traced to a typhoon around 1775 that left about 20 survivors.
Oliver Sacks himself had prosopagnosia (face blindness) and wrote about it in The Mind's Eye (2010).
After injuring his leg on a Norwegian mountain, Sacks described his leg feeling as if it no longer belonged to him.
Sacks's first book was about migraine, including its auras.
His memoir of a chemistry-mad childhood; his mother was a surgeon and his father a GP.

neuro.fact: Belief that a loved one has been replaced by an identical impostor. Described by Joseph Capgras in 1923.
Belief that different people are one person in disguise. Named after Italian quick-change actor Leopoldo Fregoli.
Belief that one is dead, rotting or missing organs ('walking corpse'). Described by Jules Cotard in 1880.
A hand acts on its own, e.g. unbuttoning a shirt the other hand is buttoning; linked to corpus callosum or frontal damage.
Cortical blindness with denial: the person is blind but insists they can see and confabulates.
After damage to the visual cortex, people can point to or avoid objects they say they cannot see.
Usually after right-brain stroke: people ignore the left side of space, eating only the right half of the plate or drawing half a clock.
After brain injury speech sounds like a foreign accent. A famous case: Astrid L., a Norwegian woman injured in a 1941 air raid, was shunned for sounding German.
Distorted perception of size or body (things look tiny or huge). Named by John Todd in 1955; linked to migraine and some infections such as glandular fever.
Hearing a loud bang or crash when falling asleep or waking. Harmless, but startling.
Sensation or pain in an amputated limb; mirror-box therapy (V.S. Ramachandran, 1990s) can ease it.
Senses cross: letters or numbers have colours, sounds have shapes. Grapheme–colour is the most common type.
Motion blindness: the world appears as a series of still frames. Famous patient L.M. found pouring tea hard because the liquid seemed frozen.
Face blindness: people recognise others by voice, gait or clothes. Can be from birth or after brain injury.
'Sleeping Beauty syndrome': episodes of sleeping up to 20 hours a day, with confusion and big appetite, mostly in teenage boys.
A rare inherited prion disease that destroys the ability to sleep and is fatal.
A prion disease among the Fore people of Papua New Guinea, spread through funeral practices; called the 'laughing death' for its uncontrolled laughter. Nobel Prize to Carleton Gajdusek (1976).
Henry Molaison had both hippocampi removed for epilepsy in 1953 and could no longer form new long-term memories, yet could learn new motor skills.
A British musician whose herpes encephalitis (1985) left him with a memory span of seconds; he could still play and conduct music.
Broca's 1861 patient could say only 'tan'; his brain showed the left frontal speech area now called Broca's area.
Described by George Huntington in 1872 at age 22; caused by a CAG repeat expansion. Folk singer Woody Guthrie had it.
The first person diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease, by Alois Alzheimer in 1906.
James Parkinson's 1817 'An Essay on the Shaking Palsy' first described it.
Named after Georges Gilles de la Tourette (1885), a student of Charcot. Coprolalia (involuntary swearing) affects only a minority.
Rare autoimmune disorder with muscle rigidity and spasms; Céline Dion shared her diagnosis in 2022.
Brain freeze's medical name is sphenopalatine ganglioneuralgia.
The sudden jolt as you fall asleep, often with a feeling of falling. Common and harmless.
Highly superior autobiographical memory: remembering what happened on almost every day of life. First described with Jill Price (2006).
Feeling touch on your own body when you see someone else being touched.
A mysterious 1917–1928 epidemic of 'sleeping sickness' affecting about a million people; the cause is still debated.

psych.fact: A shared delusion passed from one person to another close to them; described by Lasègue and Falret in 1877.
Erotomania: the belief that someone, often famous or higher status, is secretly in love with you.
Delusional jealousy about a partner's infidelity; named after Shakespeare's play.
Delusional parasitosis: the fixed belief that insects are crawling under the skin. (Ekbom also described restless legs syndrome.)
Severe self-neglect and squalor in older people, often with hoarding. Named after the Greek philosopher who lived in a barrel, although he did not hoard.
Named by Richard Asher in 1951 after Baron Munchausen, a teller of tall tales. Now called factitious disorder.
Giving approximate answers (e.g. 2 + 2 = 5); first described in prisoners by Sigbert Ganser in 1898.
Visitors to Jerusalem who develop religious delusions, e.g. believing they are a biblical figure.
Dizziness, racing heart or fainting in front of great art; named after the French writer who described it in Florence in 1817.
Distress, mostly reported in Japanese tourists, when Paris doesn't match their romantic expectations.
A culture-bound panic that the genitals are shrinking into the body; epidemics have been reported in parts of Asia.
First a medical diagnosis (Johannes Hofer, 1688) for homesick Swiss soldiers.
'On Being Sane in Insane Places': pseudo-patients faked hearing voices to get admitted. Hugely influential, but later investigations have raised serious doubts about its data.
Hat makers used mercury to treat felt; mercury poisoning (erethism) caused tremor, irritability and shyness.
In Strasbourg, hundreds of people danced for days; theories include mass psychogenic illness.
After playing a game for hours, people see its shapes when they close their eyes or as they fall asleep.
